LOS ANGELES, California (CNN) -- He is the international superstar responsible for breathing life into the iconic comic book hero Wolverine. Her movies have earned more than $2 billion worldwide, including the entire "X-Men" franchise. Hugh Jackman emerges as Wolverine in "X-Men Origins: Wolverine," which opened Friday. Actor Hugh Jackman and film producer Lauren Shuler Donner recently sat down for a candid conversation about their new film, "X-Men Origins: Wolverine." Specifically, the pair talked about the scene in which Jackman's character is transformed from a simple mutant with bony claws that periodically protrude from the back of his hands to an invincible mutant filled with an indestructible metal called adamantium. This scene represents the ultimate birth of a comic legend as the character is transformed from Logan to Wolverine.  Watch the scene in which Wolverine is unleashed » . Hugh Jackman: I knew this was the birth of the character; this is where we see him in full flight. It's called in the comic book "berserker rage." It's not really in the English language, but it may be now! But, this idea that this complete animal [has been] unleashed, which is obviously the entire story -- this battle between the animal and human is something we all relate to. Lauren Shuler Donner: There were many things he had to do in the tank, you know. One of them was he had to be lowered, and then the needles had to come towards him. Now, most of those were CGI, so he had to look in certain places where the needles were. But, he couldn't hear [director] Gavin [Hood]. So they ... tried all kinds of sounds, speakers, everything. ... They finally devised this toe method where, if Gavin pulled on Hugh's big toe, it meant the things are coming, the second toe is this, the last toe is rise up, very sophisticated. (laughter) Jackman: I had in my head that I've got to be in much better shape -- not better shape, different shape, kind of ridiculous shape because I wanted it to be uncomfortable. I wanted it to feel like I felt when I saw Robert De Niro in "Cape Fear," that -- whoa, this guy is dangerous, he's powerful, he's dangerous, and he can snap at any point. Donner: There's an iconic drawing of Wolverine coming out of the tank in the comics with the things popping out of him and his hair all over him in a rage, and we wanted to be that image. That's the image we wanted for the fans. Jackman: I was a little frightened when I watched it, like, "Is that me?" [My wife] Deb was like, "Hugh, this is ridiculous. I don't even know who that is."

**LOS ANGELES, California (CNN) --** He is the international superstar who brought the iconic comic book hero Wolverine to life. Her films—including the entire “X-Men” franchise—have earned more than $2 billion worldwide.

Hugh Jackman reprises his role as Wolverine in “X-Men Origins: Wolverine,” which opened Friday. Jackman and film producer Lauren Shuler Donner recently sat down for a candid conversation about their new film.

In particular, they discussed the scene in which Jackman’s character is transformed from a simple mutant—whose bony claws periodically protrude from the backs of his hands—into an invincible mutant infused with an indestructible metal called adamantium.

The scene marks the definitive birth of a comic book legend, as the character is transformed from Logan into Wolverine.

**Watch the scene in which Wolverine is unleashed »**

**Hugh Jackman:** I knew this was the birth of the character; this is where we see him in full flight. In the comic book, it’s called “berserker rage.” It’s not really in the English language, but it may be now!

But the idea that this complete animal has been unleashed is obviously central to the entire story. This battle between the animal and the human is something we can all relate to.

**Lauren Shuler Donner:** There were many things he had to do in the tank. One of them was being lowered while the needles moved toward him. Most of those were CGI, so he had to look in specific places where the needles were supposed to be.

But he couldn’t hear [director] Gavin [Hood], so they tried all kinds of sounds, speakers—everything. They finally devised this method using his toes: If Gavin pulled on Hugh’s big toe, it meant the needles were coming; the second toe meant this; and the last toe meant to rise up. Very sophisticated. *(Laughter)*

**Jackman:** I had it in my head that I needed to be in much better shape—not better shape, but a different kind of shape, a rather ridiculous shape—because I wanted it to be uncomfortable.

I wanted people to feel the way I did when I saw Robert De Niro in “Cape Fear”: Whoa, this guy is dangerous. He’s powerful, he’s dangerous, and he could snap at any moment.

**Donner:** There’s an iconic drawing in the comics of Wolverine emerging from the tank, with things protruding from him, his hair all over the place, and in a rage. We wanted to recreate that image. That’s the image we wanted for the fans.

**Jackman:** I was a little frightened when I watched it. I thought, “Is that me?” [My wife] Deb was like, “Hugh, this is ridiculous. I don’t even know who that is.”
outputs.L2:
LOS ANGELES, California (CNN) — Hugh Jackman became a global star by bringing the legendary comic-book character Wolverine to the screen. Producer Lauren Shuler Donner’s films—including every installment in the “X-Men” series—have generated more than $2 billion at the worldwide box office.

Jackman returns as Wolverine in “X-Men Origins: Wolverine,” which debuted Friday. He and Donner recently spoke openly about the movie, focusing on the sequence that shows Jackman’s character undergoing a dramatic transformation. Logan begins as an ordinary mutant whose bone claws occasionally extend from the backs of his hands. He is then infused with adamantium, an unbreakable metal, becoming virtually indestructible. The moment marks the definitive creation of the comic-book icon: Logan becomes Wolverine.

Watch the sequence in which Wolverine is set free »

**Hugh Jackman:** I understood that this moment was the character’s true beginning—the first time audiences would see him fully unleashed. In the comics, it’s known as “berserker rage.” That phrase may not technically be part of the English language, though perhaps it is now! The central idea is that a complete animal has been released. That is really what the whole story explores: the struggle between the human and animal sides of a person, something everyone can identify with.

**Lauren Shuler Donner:** Hugh had to perform several different actions inside the tank. He needed to be lowered into it, and then the needles had to move toward him. Most of the needles were created with CGI, so he had to direct his gaze toward places where nothing was actually there. The difficulty was that he couldn’t hear the director, Gavin Hood. They experimented with speakers, noises and all sorts of other methods. Eventually, they invented a signaling system using Hugh’s toes. If Gavin tugged on his big toe, it indicated that the needles were approaching; another toe communicated a different instruction; and pulling the final toe told him to rise. It was extremely advanced. *(laughter)*

**Jackman:** I decided I needed to look much more physically imposing—not necessarily fitter, but built in a different, almost absurd way. I wanted my appearance to make people uneasy. I was trying to recreate the feeling I had watching Robert De Niro in “Cape Fear”: the sense that this man is powerful and dangerous and could suddenly lose control at any moment.

**Donner:** The comics contain a famous image of Wolverine bursting out of the tank, with objects sticking out of his body, his hair flying everywhere and his face filled with fury. We wanted to reproduce that visual. That was the image we hoped to deliver to the fans.

**Jackman:** Seeing the finished scene was slightly alarming. I found myself wondering, “Is that really me?” My wife, Deb, said, “Hugh, this is absurd. I don’t even recognize that person.”

Hugh Jackman reprises his iconic role as Wolverine in *X-Men Origins: Wolverine*, produced by Lauren Shuler Donner. The film explores Logan’s past and depicts his transformation from a mutant with natural bone claws into Wolverine, a nearly indestructible weapon whose skeleton is infused with adamantium.

For Jackman, the pivotal transformation sequence represents Wolverine’s true birth. It is also a powerful expression of the character’s animalistic “berserker rage,” as Logan endures the agonizing procedure and emerges with heightened strength and fury.

Filming the sequence presented significant technical challenges. Jackman had to perform inside a tank while reacting to needles that would largely be added later through computer-generated effects. Because he could not hear director Gavin Hood underwater, the production team devised a practical communication method: crew members pulled on Jackman’s toes to signal when and how he should move. This unusual system allowed him to coordinate his performance during one of the film’s most physically demanding scenes.
outputs.L4:
In *X-Men Origins: Wolverine*, Hugh Jackman’s character undergoes the brutal experiment that bonds adamantium to his skeleton and transforms him into the nearly indestructible Wolverine. Jackman and producer Lauren Shuler Donner have described the challenge of filming the sequence, which required the actor to perform while submerged inside a laboratory tank. Although the finished scene shows numerous needles penetrating Logan’s body, the needles were created with CGI, allowing Jackman to move safely while still conveying the procedure’s extreme pain.

Because Jackman could not easily see or hear directions from inside the tank, the crew devised a simple physical cue: they pulled on his toe to signal when he should react. Guided by those cues, Jackman had to create the illusion that each virtual needle was entering his body. His performance depended on precise timing, intense physical control, and an ability to communicate agony despite the restrictions imposed by the water and equipment.

The experiment culminates in Logan’s apparent death, followed by his sudden, violent awakening. Bursting from the tank, he unleashes the “berserker rage” that has long defined Wolverine in the comics. The moment represents more than the acquisition of an adamantium skeleton; it is the symbolic birth of the iconic hero audiences recognize.

At the same time, the scene establishes Wolverine’s central internal conflict. Logan possesses compassion, loyalty, and a deeply human desire for connection, yet he also carries powerful animal instincts that can overwhelm him when he is frightened, hurt, or enraged. His transformation makes him physically stronger, but it also intensifies the struggle between those two sides of his nature. The sequence therefore serves as both an action spectacle and a defining character moment, showing the pain, fury, and divided identity at the heart of Wolverine.
